overview.body: This is a BUILD unit. Module 4 opens by retiring Module 3's hardest-working constants: the route distances and the destination lists for every city. The map moves out of the code and into two text files, loaded into dictionaries when the game starts. distances['San Antonio']['Houston'] is 200, and adding ten cities means adding ten lines to a file, not touching code. Everything else from Lab 3.3 carries forward: the main menu, save and load, play again, the d20, the hazards, and the trip report file. Same game, smarter data.

mentorQuote.quote: Real codebases keep data and code in separate places. If you have to edit a function every time the business changes its mind about a city, the design is wrong. Move the data into a file, load it once at startup, and let the code stay still. That's the whole point of Module 4.

content.body: A new library function, load_city_distances(). It reads city_distances.txt one line at a time and builds a nested dictionary: the outer key is the city you start from, the inner key is where you can go, and the value is the miles. The game loads it when it starts and says how many cities it found.

Lab 3.3 kept one constant per route: SAT_TO_CORPUS = 150, SAT_TO_HOUSTON = 200, and so on. That works for three cities. It doesn't work for ten cities and 24 routes, which is what this file holds. Keep the data in a file and write one function that reads it, and adding a city later means adding a line to the file, not editing code.

content.quote: If you had to add twenty more cities to this game next unit, how long would it take? If the answer is 'just add twenty lines to a text file', the design is right. If the answer is 'edit the code in five places', the design is wrong. Pick the data shape that makes the next change small.

content.title: How the Road Network Is Modeled
content.body: The 24 routes in city_distances.txt are the cities you can drive between on a Texas interstate. San Antonio reaches Corpus Christi (I-37), Houston (I-10), Austin (I-35), Laredo (I-35), and El Paso (I-10). Houston reaches Galveston (I-45) and Dallas (I-45). Austin reaches Dallas and Fort Worth by the I-35E and I-35W split. Dallas and Fort Worth connect by I-30; Dallas reaches Texarkana by I-30; Fort Worth reaches El Paso by I-20 and I-10.

items: In function_library.py, below display_numbered_list() and above the self-test main() at the bottom, add a new section. Each line of the file looks like San Antonio,Houston,200: .strip() takes the newline off the end, and .split(',') breaks the line into a list of three strings. Only the miles need int(). The first time a city shows up, it doesn't have an inner dictionary yet, so the if makes one:

content.code:
# ============================================================
# CITY DATA LOADERS (Added in Lab 4-1)
# ============================================================

def load_city_distances(filename):
    """
    Read the city routes from a file into a nested dictionary.

    Args:
        filename (str): The file to read, one city1,city2,miles per line

    Returns:
        dict: distances[city1][city2] is the miles from city1 to city2
    """
    distances = {}
    infile = open(filename, 'r')
    for line in infile:
        parts = line.strip().split(',')
        city1 = parts[0]
        city2 = parts[1]
        miles = int(parts[2])
        if city1 not in distances:
            distances[city1] = {}
        distances[city1][city2] = miles
    infile.close()
    return distances

content.code:
def load_city_info(filename):
    """
    Read each city's type and tagline from a file into a dictionary.

    Args:
        filename (str): The file to read, one city,type,tagline per line

    Returns:
        dict: info[city] is {'type': ..., 'tagline': ...}
    """
    info = {}
    infile = open(filename, 'r')
    for line in infile:
        parts = line.strip().split(',')
        city = parts[0]
        city_type = parts[1]
        tagline = parts[2]
        info[city] = {'type': city_type, 'tagline': tagline}
    infile.close()
    return info

items: In function_library.py, replace the whole DESTINATION HELPERS section, banner and all three functions, with the dictionary versions. A for loop over a dictionary goes through its keys, in the order they were added, which is the file's order. list(distances[city].keys()) lines the keys up so a menu number can pick one. The header and the menu lines print exactly as they did in Lab 3.3:

content.code:
# ============================================================
# DESTINATION HELPERS (Added in Lab 3-2, rewritten in Lab 4-1)
# ============================================================

def display_destinations(city, distances):
    """
    Show the numbered destination menu for a city.

    Args:
        city (str): The city the player is in
        distances (dict): The nested dictionary from load_city_distances()

    Returns:
        int: How many destinations the menu shows
    """
    print(f'From {city}, you can travel to:')
    option_num = 1
    for dest in distances[city]:
        miles = distances[city][dest]
        print(f'  {option_num}. {dest} - {miles} miles')
        option_num = option_num + 1
    return len(distances[city])


def get_destination(city, distances, choice):
    """
    Look up the destination for a menu choice.

    Args:
        city (str): The city the player is in
        distances (dict): The nested dictionary from load_city_distances()
        choice (int): The menu number the player chose, from 1

    Returns:
        tuple: The destination and its distance
    """
    dests = list(distances[city].keys())
    dest = dests[choice - 1]
    return dest, distances[city][dest]


def get_redirect(city, distances, avoid):
    """
    Pick a random destination other than the one the player wanted.

    Args:
        city (str): The city the player is in
        distances (dict): The nested dictionary from load_city_distances()
        avoid (str): The destination the player wanted

    Returns:
        tuple: Another destination and its distance, or the only one
        there is when the city has a single route
    """
    options = list(distances[city].keys())
    if avoid in options:
        options.remove(avoid)
    if len(options) > 0:
        index = random.randint(0, len(options) - 1)
        dest = options[index]
        return dest, distances[city][dest]
    else:
        only_option = list(distances[city].keys())[0]
        return only_option, distances[city][only_option]

# ============================================================
# CITY TYPE CHECKS (Added in Lab 4-1)
# ============================================================

def is_win_city(city, city_info):
    """
    Check whether a city is a beach that wins the game.

    Args:
        city (str): The city to check
        city_info (dict): The dictionary from load_city_info()

    Returns:
        bool: True if the city's type is 'WIN'
    """
    return city_info[city]['type'] == 'WIN'


def is_dead_end(city, city_info):
    """
    Check whether a city is a dead end: nowhere to go but home.

    Args:
        city (str): The city to check
        city_info (dict): The dictionary from load_city_info()

    Returns:
        bool: True if the city's type is 'DEAD_END' or 'WRONG_WAY'
    """
    city_type = city_info[city]['type']
    return city_type == 'DEAD_END' or city_type == 'WRONG_WAY'
